title: API Authentication
summary: Covers four levels of API access control (none, Basic, API key, Bearer token), how each is sent in a request, and the authentication vs authorization distinction. Learners first try each type in Postman against the Secrets API, then implement all four server-side with Axios.

concepts.heading: Why authenticate
points: If data is valuable, an API should check who is asking before releasing it. Failing that check gives a 401 Unauthorized response.
Four levels in increasing security: no auth, Basic auth, API key, token-based (OAuth style).
Authentication = proving who you are (login/registration). Authorization = being permitted to use the service, e.g. by holding an API key that may or may not be tied to a registered user.

concepts.heading: Level 0: no authentication
points: Easy to adopt, inclusive; typical for public read-only data (the Bored API).
Abuse is limited with rate limiting, counting requests per IP per time window (the Bored API allows 100 per 15 minutes). That caps traffic but does not identify users.

concepts.heading: Level 1: Basic authentication
points: Client supplies a username and password it registered with the provider.
Transport: the pair is joined as username:password, Base64-encoded, and sent in the Authorization header as the word Basic, a space, then the encoded string.
Base64 re-encodes the text's bytes using a 64-character alphabet; the output is slightly longer than the input (e.g. 3 chars become 4). It is an encoding, not encryption.

Demonstration: copy the header Postman generates and decode it on a Base64 decoder site to recover the plain username:password. That shows the weakness; it is acceptable only because providers serve over HTTPS, which encrypts traffic in transit.
Postman builds this header for you when Authorization type is Basic Auth (check the Headers tab). Axios does the same via its auth option.

concepts.heading: Level 2: API key
points: Provider issues a key (in the Secrets API, a GET to the generate-api-key endpoint). The key goes with every request.
Placement depends on the API: sometimes a header, sometimes a query parameter. Read the docs. Here it is a query parameter named apiKey (capital K).

Benefits: provider can track and bill usage per key (e.g. Google Maps APIs bill by request count), cap usage, revoke and regenerate keys. A leaked key does not expose the user's password or payment details.
Secrets API /filter takes score (minimum embarrassment score, 1-10) plus apiKey.

concepts.heading: Level 3: token-based (Bearer) auth and OAuth
points: User logs in once with username and password, the server issues a token, and the token alone is used for later calls. The API (and any third-party app) never handles the password afterwards.

OAuth 2.0 is the industry standard: a third-party app (e.g. weather app reading a user's calendar) sends the user to 'sign in with Google'; Google issues a token the app uses to act for that user within granted permissions.
In the Secrets API: POST username and password (form-urlencoded) to get-auth-token. Calling again returns the already-issued token.
Send it as header Authorization: Bearer <token> (capital B, one space). Used for GET /secrets/{id}.
Postman: Authorization type Bearer Token generates that header.

concepts.heading: Pagination (side note)
points: GET /all returns secrets 10 per page and accepts a page query parameter, so huge result sets are sent in slices.

concepts.heading: Postman walk-through (Secrets API at secrets-api.appbrewery.com)
points: Register: POST /register, body type x-www-form-urlencoded with keys username and password. Status 200 means success; keep the credentials.
Basic: GET /all (try page=2), Authorization tab type Basic Auth with those credentials.
API key: GET generate-api-key, then GET /filter?score=7 with apiKey as a query param (Postman Authorization tab 'API Key', add to Query Params).
Bearer: POST get-auth-token with credentials, then GET /secrets/2 with Bearer Token auth.

concepts.heading: Code with Axios
points: No auth: await axios.get(API_URL + "/random"), then pass JSON.stringify(result.data) to the EJS view as content (just to display text).
Basic: second argument { auth: { username, password } }; Axios Base64-encodes and sets the header.
API key: second argument { params: { score: 5, apiKey } }, or write the query string into the URL. Both are valid.
Bearer: a config object { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } } as second argument.
Each route is wrapped in try/catch; on failure the reference sends status 404 with error.message.

pitfalls: Base64 is reversible by anyone; Basic auth over plain HTTP exposes the password.
Bearer header format must be exactly 'Bearer ' plus the token; a missing space or lowercase scheme can fail.
API key placement varies: query param vs header. Wrong location gives 401/403.

Never commit real usernames, passwords, keys or tokens. The reference repo hard-codes the author's real values in index.js and solution.js; those are omitted here. (Extra) Load them from a .env file with dotenv instead.
Reference quirk: its index.js fetches /secrets/2 while the starter comment asks for another id; and error handling just returns the Axios message with a 404 status regardless of the real cause.
Reusing /get-auth-token returns the same token, so a 'new' token not appearing is normal.

gaps_and_ideas: New lesson 'API authentication' with blurb: prove who you are to an API via Basic, API key or Bearer token.

Tasks: (1) Base64-encode 'user:pass' with btoa and build a Basic header by hand; (2) send an API key as query param vs header; (3) add a Bearer header via an axios config object; (4) read a 401 response and display a message; (5) move secrets into environment variables.
Starter code: an Express file with four empty routes and placeholder constants.

Interactive demo: a mock API panel where the learner picks an auth type, sees the exact request headers/query that would be sent, a live Base64 encode/decode box, and the mock server's 200 or 401 response.
